title: Largest Number Matching Its Own Count
statement:
You get an array arr of positive integers. Call a value self-counting if it appears in the array exactly as many times as the value itself. For example, 3 is self-counting if there are exactly three 3s.

Return the largest self-counting value, or -1 if there is none.

examples.why: 1 appears once, 2 twice and 3 three times. All three are self-counting; the largest is 3.
5 appears twice and 4 three times. Neither count matches its value.
2 appears three times, which is too many. 1 appears once, so it is the answer even though it is smaller.

hints: You need to know how many times each value appears.
Count every value once in a single pass, instead of rescanning the array for each value.
With a map (or an array indexed by value) of counts, check every value v where count[v] equals v and keep the biggest.

explain.intuition:
The question is about counts, so count first. One pass fills a map from value to number of appearances. Then walk the map and keep the largest value whose count equals itself.

A value can only be self-counting if it appears at most n times, so values above n can never qualify. That lets you use a plain array of size n + 1 instead of a hash map, which is the same trick as a counting sort.
steps: Create count, an array of size n + 1 filled with 0.
For each value v, if v ≤ n add 1 to count[v]. Larger values cannot qualify.
Walk v from n down to 1 and return the first v with count[v] === v.
pitfalls: Returning the first self-counting value you meet in the array instead of the largest one.
Treating "appears at least v times" as good enough. In [2, 2, 2, 1] the 2 appears three times and does not count.

solutions.title: Recount for every value
solutions.idea: For each element, scan the whole array to count it. Simple, but quadratic.

solutions.title: Count array
solutions.idea: Only values up to n can qualify, so count them in an array and scan it from the top.

followups: The array is a stream you can only read once and n is unknown. What do you store?
Return all self-counting values in increasing order instead of only the largest.
